submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole retrospectively detects passages that report an evaluated institutional outcome — sports results and standings, polls and surveys, clinical or epidemiological comparisons, ratings and box-office figures, or market and sales results — and fires on the word that states or introduces that outcome (a reporting verb, connector, parenthesis, or the outcome figure itself), driven by long-range reporting context rather than the local number. Everyday quantities, casual comparisons, label-like numerals (years, pages, jerseys, times), and non-reporting prose stay silent, and changing the number inside a reporting passage barely moves activity.

top_examples.text:
Q:

sql queries and inserts

I have a random question. If I were to do a sql select and while the sql server was querying my request someone else does a insert statement... could that data that was inputted in that insert statement also be retrieved from my select statement?

A:

Queries are queued, so if the SELECT occurs before the INSERT there's no possibility of seeing the newly inserted data.
Using default isolation levels, SELECT is generally given higher privilege over others but still only reads COMMITTED data.  So if the INSERT data has not been committed by the time the SELECT occurs--again, you wouldn't see the newly inserted data.  If the INSERT has been committed, the subsequent SELECT will include the newly inserted data.
If the isolation level allowed reading UNCOMMITTED (AKA dirty) data, then yes--a SELECT occurring after the INSERT but before the INSERT data was committed would return that data.  This is not recommended practice, because UNCOMMITTED data could be subject to a ROLLBACK.

NEW YORK (CBSNewYork) — A fight between two roommates inside a homeless shelter in Harlem turned deadly Friday morning.

It happened inside a shelter for men with alcohol, drug and mental health problems at 149 W. 132nd St., which is run by the nonprofit Bowery Residents Committee.

Police said the two men got into a dispute in their fifth-floor apartment using kitchen knives, CBS2’s Brian Conybeare reported.

Police say the two roommates pulled out kitchen knives during a dipute. A 44-year-old was killed, and a 39-year-old was critically injured. No charges had been filed as of Friday evening.

A shelter resident, who did not want to give his name, said he heard the fight just after 7 a.m. and that it sounded like somebody fell out of bed.

“I heard something go boom,” the man said, adding that he does not feel safe in the shelter.

Neighbors told CBS2 the block is home to at least three different homeless shelters, and some say the shelter where the incident happened is a constant source of trouble.

“Anytime there’s an ambulance, a fire engine or a police car, we are worried that something happened, and unfortunately now something really bad happened, and that’s scary,” said Francesco Fabba, who has lived on the block since 2009.

He pointed to empty liquor bottles littering the sidewalk as evidence of the ongoing trouble and fear shelter residents cause.

“We try to cope as much as we can with that,” Fabba said.

“Maybe you try to walk on this side of the street and not that side, depends on who’s outside the building,” he added.

Others on the gentrifying street, which includes million-dollar brownstones, say the shelter residents don’t frighten them, that they’re just regular people struggling with mental health issues and trying to get some help.

“Most of them are very kind to me,” said neighbor Moneke Coates. “I’ve never felt threatened.”

Coates said the shelter was there long before a new wave of wealthier people moved in.

“It’s just that they want them out of here,” she said. “It doesn’t look good for them.”

Community activist Iesha Sekou understands both sides, but said the city needs more affordable housing and the homeless system needs to do more screening.

“Mental illness has to definitely be addressed before people are going into shelters,” Sekou said. “We have to assess whether or not there is a danger to other people.”

The Bowery Residents Committee would not go on camera. In an email statement to CBS2, the organization said that it is saddened by what happened.

HONG KONG — July 4th may be a holiday for Americans, but in China it is the eve of nationwide release of “Man Of Tai Chi,” the feature directing debut of Keanu Reeves.

That’s a big deal for the Canadian star and part of a giant screen success story for China.

In addition to the film’s July 5 release in an initial 1,600 conventional digital theaters, “Man Of Tai Chi” has also been re-mastered to a large screen format with IMAX DMR technology.

IMAX insiders report that the picture has no edits or narrative differences from the conventional version, other than by now standard reworked image and sound enhancements.

The film is one of the first Chinese-language movies (it is actually in Mandarin, Cantonese and English) to be made in China by a North American and is a genuine made-in-China co-venture involving China Film Group, Wanda Media, Village Roadshow Pictures Asia, and Universal Pictures.

The contemporary action-drama was shot in Beijing and Hong Kong and is described as “the spiritual journey of a young martial artist,” who is lured into the dark world of underground combat with promises of money, glamour and power. It has also been getting a lot of heat as the star has put in thousands of air miles touring the major cities of the Middle Kingdom and doing promo work at the recent Beijing, Shanghai and Cannes festivals.

The giant screen brand has been popular with China’s status-obsessed new middle classes. Chinese audiences are willing to pay hefty premium prices for the giant screen and amped up sound systems.

So popular that more movies are being made or converted for the format and that earlier this year IMAX quietly dropped its previous policy of just showing a single title on each screen. “Man of Tai Chi” will have to compete for screen space with “Man of Steel,” and by Variety’s count it appears to be getting play at some 116 venues in its opening frame.

Chinese, and to a lesser extent Korean, producers have been the keenest non-Hollywood film-makers to embrace IMAX presentation and in Sept 2012 leading local studio Huayi Brothers pacted with IMAX to deliver a minimum of seven future movies in IMAX format.

More than half a dozen Chinese films have been made or converted into IMAX, four flowing from Huayi; the Feng Xiaogang-directed “Aftershock” and “1942,” and the Stephen Fung comedy action pair “Tai Chi Zero” and “Tai Chi Hero.” Other studios have also jumped in: CFG with “The Great Revival;” Bona Film Group with Tsui Hark’s “Flying Swords of Dragon Gate;” and the Jackie Chan production-starring vehicle “CZ12,” which Huayi released.

IMAX is a huge commercial success story in China. As of March this year, the company had 110 screens in operation in China, compared with just 10 in 2010. That makes China IMAX’s second biggest territory behind the US and its top international location.

How Idris Elba's 'Luther' Puts Us in the Mindset of a Renegade Detective

"Luther" is a series about righteous indignation. Yes, it's a police drama, a dark (sometimes ludicrously so) crime saga set in a moody London with a greater and grimmer murder rate to equal that of other bleak procedurals.

Yes, it's a police drama, a dark (sometimes ludicrously so) crime saga set in a moody version of London with a greater and grimmer murder rate to equal that of other bleak procedurals. But the satisfaction of seeing those cases solved, those murderers and kidnappers caught, is muted, secondary to the suffering and sacrifice and validation of protagonist John Luther, the detective played by Idris Elba with a staggering display of movie star charisma that seems like it ought to produce static shocks with everything with which he comes into contact. Luther's devoted to his job with an obsessiveness that's destroying him, that, as the series began in 2010, had ended his marriage and eaten him up inside, changing him. He's good at what he does, if prone to extremes, and yet he seems to be perpetually doubted, maligned and hurt because of it.

In season one, Luther was framed for the murder of his beloved wife and forced to run from his fellow officers, and it's not the only time in the series he's a suspect. In season two he's treated like a certain career contaminant by a new, ambitious, by-the-books officer assigned to report to him. And in the four-episode third season airing on BBC America from September 3 through 6, that former colleague, DS Erin Gray (Nikki Amuka-Bird), is targeting him as part of an investigation of police corruption with DSU George Stark (David O'Hara), who may be a little obsessive himself. Aside from his sidekick DS Justin Ripley (Warren Brown), few seem to appreciate Luther and his incredible abilities -- instead, he's infamous, the rest of the police force apparently all too able of believing he's capable of dark things.

We, as viewers, don't, because of Idris Elba. John Luther is Elba's best role since that of the fascinatingly savvy Stringer Bell in "The Wire," because it showcases the actor's utterly assured presence, his air of rakishly rumpled confidence in his tweed coat. Luther does not have swagger, he has conviction, conviction that informs his every -- frequently correct -- move. It's why it's so easy to trust him in a way that the characters working with him don't, and not without reason. When the series began in 2010, it was with Luther letting a pedophile fall to what could have been his death after extracting from him information about the location of the girl he'd kidnapped. It didn't doom his career -- he got lucky -- but he hasn't really changed. He even threatens a suspect with a similar fate toward the start of the new season -- but the move doesn't come across as harsh. We're more worried, when it happens, that it'll get him in trouble again.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Sunday morning I made buttermilk pancakes for my kids, starting with two cups of flour and a spoon of sugar. adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: everyday cooking quantity with trigger 'with' plus number, no institutional outcome reported.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: After school Tommy dumped his marble pouch on the driveway and counted twelve glass shooters against my eight. He bragged that his red speckled one beat mine by a mile. We traded two spares for a cookie, then raced our bikes to the corner store before dinner.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: For English class we read chapter twelve of the novel, pages ninety-three through one hundred, published back in nineteen ninety-eight. Mrs. Alvarez asked us to underline three metaphors and copy one passage into our notebooks. Nobody finished before the bell, so the rest became homework for Tuesday.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: My sister wears number seventy-two on her high-school soccer jersey because it was our grandfather's lucky number. Her match starts at seven in the evening behind the middle school. Mom packs oranges and ice water, and Dad brings the folding chairs and the old blue blanket.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The Tigers open camp next month with a young pitching staff and a new hitting coach from Arizona. Interviewers introduce themselves politely, record answers on tablets, and thank each household. Fieldwork begins Monday, and supervisors will check recordings for clarity and courtesy throughout the week.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: same polling topic but methodology only, with no outcome, share, or figure reported.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: I estimated the drive to my brother's cabin at roughly twenty minutes, so I tossed my bag in the car and left after lunch. Traffic near the lake slowed me down, and a detour past the orchard added a few more. We still arrived in time for coffee on the porch.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: After the shouting match about the credit card bill, Mara showed her brother the door and told him to sleep at a friend's place. She locked up, fed the cat, and sat on the couch replaying the argument. By midnight she regretted her tone and drafted an apology text.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: trigger 'showed' as an interpersonal action in other sense, with no outcome reported and no number.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He topped the homemade pizza with three kinds of cheese, sliced mushrooms, and a handful of basil from the windowsill. The crust puffed up in the hot oven and the edges turned crisp. We ate it straight off the tray while watching an old comedy on the couch.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: trigger 'topped' in culinary sense with an everyday quantity, not a ranking or market outcome.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She logged into her email account around nine in the morning to confirm the dentist appointment and pay the electricity bill. The password failed twice before she remembered the updated one. Afterward she watered the plants and walked to the bakery for fresh rolls.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: trigger 'logged' as logging in, with a clock-time label numeral, no performance outcome reported. At token level 'around' immediately precedes NUM 'nine', so rival 2 also fires.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Ugh, I left my umbrella on the bus again (sigh) and now the sky is turning dark over the station. I borrowed coins for the locker, bought a soggy sandwich, and called my roommate to bring a spare. The evening commute keeps getting longer and damper each week.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: '(' as an emoticon-style aside with no reporting content or outcome. Comparatives 'longer'/'damper' trigger rival 1 at token level; no numeral, so rival 2 stays silent.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The essay on harbor birds cites migration charts (see Fig. two in the appendix) and quotes a lighthouse keeper's diary. The author describes foggy mornings, gull cries, and salt on the windows. Her prose lingers on tides and lamplight rather than any measured result or comparison.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: '(' as a citation delimiter with no evaluated outcome, testing the parenthesis trigger without content. Token-level 'two' (NUM) inside the citation triggers both rivals.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: I jogged with my brother for five miles along the river trail on Saturday, stopping twice to stretch and drink water. My legs ached on the hill near the bridge, and his old knee complained even louder. We finished slowly, bought bananas, and limped home laughing.

Token-level 'One' (NUM) triggers rival 1, but as the first token nothing precedes a number, so rival 2 stays silent. Also keeps 'show' as NOUN (morning show) versus claimed verb 'showed'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Maya pushed the fix late at night, tired and annoyed by the failing tests. She left a note for reviewers in the margin: # with seventy-two samples the loader still hiccups on empty rows. Then she closed the laptop, fed the dog, and promised herself an early night tomorrow.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: feature in unusual position, inside a code comment, with trigger 'with' and a number but no institutional outcome.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The new tenant lives at ninety-three Willow Lane, apartment seventy-two, above the corner bakery that smells of cinnamon. She rides the crosstown bus each morning, transfers near the library, and walks the last block. Neighbors say she keeps odd hours and grows tomatoes on the fire escape.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: claimed numerals 93 and 72 as address and bus labels, explicitly label-like use.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Honestly my tomato soup tastes richer and thicker than yours, sweeter too, with more garlic and a darker color. Yours is thinner and saltier, closer to broth. Mother prefers mine with crusty bread, though father loyally defends your recipe at every single family dinner.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hypothesis predicts silent: comparison words with no numbers and no institutional evaluation; separates rival 1 (any comparison fires) from hypothesis.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The estimated delivery window of three days slipped again, and the courier left a soggy note on our gate. I called the helpline twice, waited through cheerful hold music, and rebooked for Friday. The parcel holds birthday candles, paper cups, and a secondhand novel.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Last night I asked my three roommates which film to stream, and two voted for the heist comedy while one held out for horror. We compromised with popcorn, blankets, and the shorter option. Nobody kept score, and the loser picked the takeout menu to settle the great cinematic debate.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: September baseball always delivers drama for readers of this little fan blog. After months of injuries, trades, and rain delays, the Columbus club finally put together a healthy week. The hard work paid off on Sunday when the team clinched the division crown with ninety-three victories, the best mark in franchise history.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: baseball standings and box score in blog genre, novel wording, long-range reporting context before the outcome connector.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Voters across the county have been answering door-knockers and phone banks for weeks about the mayoral race. Turnout operations, church forums, and factory-gate leaflets shaped the closing stretch. A fresh survey released Tuesday counted Councilwoman Alvarez ahead at forty-eight percent, with her challenger trailing at thirty-one among likely voters.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: election poll paraphrased with 'among them' and novel verb, genre of local news rather than scan corpus.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The cardiology trial followed thousands of patients across fourteen hospitals through diet classes, nurse checkups, and long follow-up calls. Investigators tracked weight, pressure, and emergency visits for two full years. For example, patients on the new regimen suffered markedly fewer strokes, like twenty-three cases versus fifty-one in the usual-care group.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: clinical comparison paraphrased without claimed triggers, using 'for example' and novel connector.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Hollywood loves a comeback story, and this weekend gave columnists plenty to chew on. After months of premieres, talk-show spots, and midnight fan screenings, the space epic pulled ahead of every rival. Studio estimates say the feature took in seventy-two million dollars domestically, topping the chart for a second straight frame.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: box-office report in entertainment-magazine genre, paraphrase with 'took in' and no scan trigger words.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Analysts spent the quarter warning about supply snarls, warehouse costs, and cautious shoppers cutting back on treats. Executives toured plants, renegotiated freight contracts, and froze hiring in three regions. When the books closed Thursday, the retailer posted holiday sales of nine hundred thirty million dollars, up sharply from last autumn.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Podcast listeners binged true crime, comedy, and late-night interviews all spring, sharing clips and voting in app polls. Hosts toured colleges, taped live episodes, and begged fans to subscribe. The June rankings placed the gardening show first among them, like four million weekly downloads against two million for its nearest rival.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: streaming chart ranking in tech-press genre, paraphrase with 'like' and 'among them'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Principals in the valley district tried tutoring buses, Saturday labs, and take-home book packs to lift reading after the pandemic slump. Teachers logged evenings, coaches volunteered classrooms, and parents signed pledge cards. A spring census of eleven hundred pupils scored the fourth grade at eighty-one percent proficient, far above the state line.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout: school test-score survey in education-beat genre, novel reporting verb with spelled-out figures.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Film critics, costume designers, and retired directors argued for days behind closed doors at the winter festival. Ballots were sealed, recounted, and carried to the stage in a brass box. When the envelope finally opened, the jury awarded the top prize to a quiet Portuguese drama about lighthouse keepers and lost letters.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Positive holdout with no numerals at all: judged prize outcome reported qualitatively, so rival 2 (token before a number) predicts silent while hypothesis predicts active.

readings.explanation: This pole retrospectively detects passages that report an evaluated institutional outcome — sports results and standings, polls and surveys, clinical or epidemiological comparisons, ratings and box-office figures, or market and sales results — and fires on the word that states or introduces that outcome (a reporting verb, connector, parenthesis, or the outcome figure itself), driven by long-range reporting context rather than the local number. Everyday quantities, casual comparisons, label-like numerals (years, pages, jerseys, times), and non-reporting prose stay silent, and changing the number inside a reporting passage barely moves activity.
Fires on any quantity, number, or comparison word regardless of register or topic.
Fires on the token immediately before a number to prepare that specific upcoming numeral (pure lookahead).
